A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DynaMath study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reordering and additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM accuracy and repetition-consistency measurements, a human evaluation, and quantitative and qualitative failure analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds an expanded human study, prompting and in-context experiments, circular-consistency testing, and further failure analyses.

M1.justification: The Python-based question-generation pipeline, 470 programs with generated images and 31 with fixed images, and core answer-extraction procedure remain unchanged. The additional prompts and demonstrations are evaluation interventions, without a revision to the proposed benchmark-generation method.

E1.justification: The reported 501-seed benchmark, nine mathematical topics, and educational levels remain. Appendix H.8 adds testing under circular permutations of multiple-choice answers, extending input-perturbation coverage. Table 1 revises answer-type categories and counts, but does not establish new underlying mathematical tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 newly include Qwen2-VL-72B in the three-shot CoT comparison, which previously covered only the three closed-source models. The original 14-model roster and human comparator are retained.

E3.justification: Human evaluation expands from 501 questions and 10 participants to 1,002 questions and 20 participants. Appendix H adds alternative prompting, variants 1–3 as demonstrations for variant 4, an identical-question control, and choice-order testing. Table 6 also changes Claude's maximum tokens from 8,192 to 1,024 and non-Qwen open-source models from 2,048 to 1,024; the PDFs do not establish whether retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix H substantially extends the analysis with failures broken down by difficulty and topic, alternative-prompt tests, further memorization cases, an in-context data-leakage proxy with a control, and circular-consistency testing. H.1's variation-type analysis is relocated from v1 Figure 4 and is not a new experiment.

E5.justification: Appendix H.7 and Table 10 newly report variance of average accuracy for four models over five evaluations of 501 questions. v1 already reported five-repetition consistency, so this establishes additional statistical reporting, not an increase in repetitions. No confidence intervals or formal significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v2 adds Qwen2-VL-72B three-shot results of 52.4% average and 22.8% worst-case accuracy, detailed robustness results, and new Appendix H experimental outcomes. Human accuracy changes from 75.8% to 77.3% under the expanded protocol; original VLM entries in Tables 2–3 remain numerically unchanged. Reported robustness values and rankings are revised, and error-analysis prose is corrected to match Figure 6, including figure-reading errors from 32.2% to 33.1%.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 defining average and worst-case accuracy, reasoning robustness, and repetition consistency are mathematically unchanged. Equation 1 is reformatted, and retained appendix solution derivations are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The benchmark's novelty, central contributions, and finding of poor robustness across question variants remain. The abstract and introduction qualify the randomness claim: failures change from being described as not due to inherent randomness to not only or not solely due to it.

C2.justification: Appendix A expands the retained difficulty limitation with seed-selection and topic bias, the absence of combined variation types, and scalability and quality-control constraints. Appendix H adds interpretations of prompting, topic-specific failures, and choice-order consistency. It explicitly acknowledges that the in-context leakage proxy cannot resolve vulnerability to pretraining or fine-tuning contamination.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit statement that the dataset is open-sourced, documents the alternative reasoning prompt and control construction, and expands the displayed few-shot template. Table 6 revises token budgets. Model identifiers, standard answer prompts, and zero-temperature decoding were already documented in v1 Appendix B.

R1.justification: Related work newly discusses MMBench and its study of answer-choice ordering. Appendix A adds references on adversarial robustness, reinforcement learning, and trustworthy language models. The principal positioning against static visual-math benchmarks and dynamic text-only benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained with local editing, updated headers and acknowledgments, and a new reproducibility statement. Limitations and future work move into Appendix A, demonstration and error-example sections are reordered, and additional experiments are organized into Appendix H. The overall narrative remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Visual reporting expands through the main-text variation montage, failure-breakdown plots, memorization screenshots, and Tables 7–10. The reasoning-robustness graphic is redrawn, with its variation-type panel relocated from v1 Figure 4 to v2 Figure 12. Tables 1–3 gain categories or rows, while many existing appendix examples are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the existing study through additional prompt and contamination controls, a larger human evaluation, clearer limitations, and corrections to textual results that previously disagreed with tables or figures. These improve evidential support and interpretation. The gains remain qualified: contamination testing is only an in-context proxy, revised token limits are not explained as corrections or reruns, and Table 10's variance units are unclear.
